title: The North Face Mountain 25 review: the two-person four-season tent owners keep for 15 years
dek: A bombproof two-person mountain tent with DAC Featherlite NSL poles. Owners report it barely moving in 75–85 mph winds. It's heavy and slow to pitch.
subject: The North Face Mountain 25
verdict: The Mountain 25 is one of the most trusted two-person four-season tents: owners describe it as bombproof in gales and heavy snow, and many have used theirs for 10 to 15 years. The trade-offs are weight, a slow pitch with cold hands, and a warm interior in summer.
bestFor: Winter camping, high-alpine and mountaineering trips, anyone who wants one tent for the worst weather they'll see.
notFor: Three-season backpacking, ultralight trips, and hot summer nights.
pros: Owner at 12,000 ft reports it barely moved in 75–85 mph winds
Two doors with vestibules good for cooking and gear
Room for two six-footers and their gear
cons: Heavy, about 8 lb 13 oz trail weight
Slow, fiddly pitch with numb hands; easier with two people
Too warm and poorly breathing for summer
Some owners report tears at pole guides or snapped pole joints
body:
## The short version

The Mountain 25 replaced The North Face's original Mountain tent and has been in the line, in updated forms, for decades. It's a two-person, four-season tent with DAC Featherlite NSL aluminum poles, and its reputation comes from owners: reviewers on Trailspace call it bombproof, and several have used theirs for 10 to 15 years or more.

## Wind and snow

This is where it earns its reputation. Most owners report excellent performance in gales, blizzards and heavy snow. One camped at 12,000 feet in 75 to 85 mph winds and said it barely moved. The caveat is pitching in that wind: several owners say it's hard to get up in a strong blow, especially alone.

## Condensation and warmth

Owners disagree here. Several report staying dry with no condensation, even in frost and heavy rain. Others say it breathes poorly and is too warm for summer. Two mesh doors and roof vents help. One owner notes the floor isn't fully waterproof in slushy spring or autumn snow, so a footprint is worth it.

## Setup

Expect five to six aluminum poles through fly sleeves, and about 20 minutes once you know it. Owners call it slow and fiddly with numb hands, and cold can stiffen the shock cord. Two people make it much easier.

## Space

Owners describe room for two six-foot people plus gear, with good pockets. The two vestibules are praised for cooking and storage, though some wish they were bigger and want a spindrift collar.

## Poles and parts

The Mountain 25 uses **9 mm** tubing, **DAC Featherlite NSL aluminum**.

Some of these figures come from owner reports rather than the published spec sheet.

One owner reported repeatedly snapping aluminum pole joints, and the frame relies on every pole being sound in high wind. Check each ferrule for cracks before a winter trip, and carry a repair sleeve.

The North Face doesn't publish pole lengths. To match a replacement, lay your pole out straight, measure tip to tip, count the sections, and read the diameter printed near a joint (or use calipers). Then search the Mountain 25 in our [pole and parts finder](/poles?model=Mountain%2025), compare against measured stock in the [pole size chart](/poles/sizes), or search by measurement in [find a pole by size](/poles/size).

## Bottom line

If your trips include real winter or above-treeline weather, the Mountain 25 is a proven choice that lasts. For three-season trips it's more tent, and more weight, than you need.
